doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Subsidiary Local 6 for black musicians
summary: Black musicians had a subsidiary card with no vote, access or committee representation; Curtis Lowe wrote a history.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well you had, earlier on, before we were actually rolling, you had told me about the integration of the musicians’ union. I’m not sure integration is the right word.
Merging. And it’s a fascinating story. And if you don’t mind repeating it.

Well sure. As a matter of fact I have some documentation that I can get to you. Curtis Lowe who was assistant to our Secretary/Treasurer, they commissioned him to document it, and he wrote a very, very nice documentation. It gives the local number of the first local, the first black local. And then he goes into the merger and it’s very well put. He doesn’t call names and stuff. But as I was saying before, see when I joined in 1937 the African-American black musicians, we had to join a Subsidiary Local. You got a card, Local 6 but Subsidiary across it. So that meant that you didn’t have access to the building, you didn’t have access to — well any of the services. But you were bound to observe their weighed scale working conditions. They had no vote in the election, and you had no representation on any committee — the wage scale committee — any of the committees. As a matter of fact at first when I joined we used to meet at the home of our Secretary/Treasurer/Business Agent. He had a room — well let me backtrack. When I first joined we met in Oakland at the Elks. But then it was when we became chartered in 1945 at 669 that we met at the Secretary/Treasurer’s business office, I mean his home, he had a room downstairs. But we met in Oakland at the Elks, it was a black Elks over there. And the jobs — we had a Business Agent, we had a President, we had a Secretary, well Secretary, the Treasurer/Business Agent, he was all the same. Secretary/Treasurer/Business Agent. So we had an official family. And we didn’t have a Board of Directors I don’t think. No I don’t think we had a Board of Directors. In ’45 when we became chartered as 669 we had a Board of Directors.
